sections.h2: Where is Columbus, Indiana, and who lives there?
sections.html:
Columbus is the county seat of Bartholomew County, about 40 miles south of Indianapolis on the East Fork of the White River. The Census Bureau estimates 52,655 residents as of July 1, 2025, and Wikipedia lists the 2020 count at 50,474 and ranks it 20th among Indiana cities.

The city covers about 28.75 square miles at an elevation of 627 feet, well below Bloomington and Carmel. The low elevation is why water is a recurring theme in local property decisions.

Roughly four in ten Columbus homes are rented, so many sellers here are landlords or heirs of rental property.

sections.h2: Did the 2008 flood affect Columbus houses?
sections.html:
Yes. On June 7, 2008, more than 10 inches of rain fell into watersheds that flow into Bartholomew County, and The Republic reports the flood caused more than $500 million in damage and claimed three lives. Roughly 2,800 homes in the county were damaged, including 15% of all structures in the city, and about 1,000 residents went to shelters.

Bartholomew County sits where the Driftwood River, Flatrock River, Clifty Creek and Haw Creek converge to form the East Fork White River. About 2,000 square miles of upstream land drains through the area, which keeps flooding among the most significant natural threats.

Planning changed afterward. The city, Columbus Regional Hospital and Cummins paid for their own floodplain study of Haw Creek because the 2008 flooding was worse than FEMA's maps predicted, and the county now has eight stream gauges. The Republic also says city officials increased local regulations on the most sensitive part of floodplains.

  • Ask whether your lot is in a mapped floodplain or floodway.
  • Keep any flood insurance claim records and repair receipts.
  • Tell any buyer about past water in the basement or crawl space.

The numbers come from The Republic's 2023 look back at the flood.

sections.h2: What is Columbus known for, and what does it mean for older homes?
sections.html:
Columbus is nicknamed "Athens on the Prairie" for its modern architecture, and Wikipedia says seven buildings built between 1942 and 1965 are National Historic Landmarks. Among them are Eero Saarinen's Irwin Union Bank, dedicated in 1954, and First Christian Church, designed by Eliel Saarinen and dedicated in 1942.

The town dates to 1820, when General John Tipton and Luke Bonesteel bought the land. It was renamed Columbus on March 20, 1821, incorporated as a town in 1864 and as a city in 1921. The first railroad in Indiana reached Columbus from Madison in 1844.

Ordinary houses are a different matter. A 1950s or 1960s ranch in Columbus is likely a conventional house, and buyers financing with a loan may ask for a new roof, furnace or electrical panel. A cash buyer looks at the same house and prices the work in.

Cummins is headquartered in Columbus and is, per Wikipedia, by far the region's largest employer. Infotech Park accounts for many research jobs, and Toyota Material Handling's North American headquarters is just south of the city.

The city's education options include Indiana University Columbus, an Ivy Tech campus, a Purdue Polytechnic campus and an Indiana Wesleyan University education center. Public schools are run by the Bartholomew Consolidated School Corporation, with Columbus North and Columbus East as the two public high schools.

One large employer affects a housing market in a particular way. When a plant changes hours or a family takes a transfer, houses show up on the market at the same time. Sellers who need to move quickly have fewer buyers to choose from.

sections.h2: Which roads and local offices matter when selling a Columbus house?
sections.html:
Interstate 65 bypasses Columbus to the west, U.S. 31 runs through the northeastern part, and Indiana Route 46 crosses the southern section. A ColumBUS service runs five routes Monday through Saturday, and Indianapolis International Airport is about 55 miles northwest.

Permits and code enforcement are split between offices, which can confuse a seller:

  • The Bartholomew County Department of Technical Code Enforcement (812-379-1535) issues building permits and inspections for new single-family homes, additions and interior remodels.
  • The Columbus-Bartholomew County Planning Department (812-376-2550) handles zoning, variances and signs.
  • City of Columbus Code Enforcement (812-376-2520) handles inoperable vehicles, unsafe homes and nuisance properties in the city limits.
  • The Engineering Department (812-376-2540) covers storm water, driveways and street access.

The city's Development and Building Services page lists each office.

sections.h2: What does the Columbus climate do to a house?
sections.html:
Columbus averages 47.34 inches of precipitation and 16.3 inches of snow a year, according to NOAA 1991 to 2020 figures cited by Wikipedia. July's average high is 86.1°F and January's average low is 21.5°F.

That mix of heavy rain, hot summers and freezing winters is hard on roofs, gutters, basements and exterior paint. Water is the common thread, so a cash buyer looks closely at the foundation, the sump and any staining on basement walls.

The city also has more than 700 acres of parks with over 20 miles of People Trails, which many buyers like. Those details add appeal but they do not offset deferred maintenance.

Yes. A February 2018 ordinance covers all residential rental property inside the city limits, and the fee is $5 per parcel of residential rental property owned. Applications are due within 30 days of purchase or ownership change.

That 30-day rule matters if you are selling or buying a rental. A buyer who closes on a rented house has a month to register it, and Community Development, reachable at (812) 376-2520, takes applications through OpenGov, the city's online system.

If you own several rentals, each parcel counts separately. If you are inheriting a rental, add registration to the list of things the estate needs to handle. Read the city's rental registration page for current details.

sections.h2: When is Bartholomew County property tax due, and what happens at closing?
sections.html:
Indiana property tax is paid in two installments, normally May 10 and November 10, and the state lists a 5 percent penalty within 30 days of a due date and 10 percent after that. Your statement with upcoming dates arrives in spring.

At closing, the title company prorates the taxes between you and the buyer. Ask for the figure ahead of time so you are not surprised on the settlement statement. Read the state due dates page.

We buy Columbus houses as-is for cash, with no lender, so closing can be fast when the title work is clean.

faqs.q: What is the median home value in Columbus, Indiana?
faqs.a: The Census Bureau lists $244,200 as the median value of owner-occupied housing units for 2020 to 2024. A specific house may be well above or below that.

faqs.q: Is Columbus, Indiana at risk of flooding?
faqs.a: Parts of it are. The June 2008 flood damaged about 15% of all structures in the city, and local officials say the area remains vulnerable. Check FEMA flood maps and the city planning office for your address.

faqs.q: Do I have to register a rental house in Columbus?
faqs.a: Yes. The 2018 ordinance covers all residential rental property in the city limits. The fee is $5 per parcel, and applications are due within 30 days of purchase or ownership change.

faqs.q: Who issues building permits in Columbus?
faqs.a: The Bartholomew County Department of Technical Code Enforcement issues building permits and inspections for new homes, additions and interior remodels. The city planning department handles zoning matters.

faqs.q: Can I sell a flood-damaged house in Columbus?
faqs.a: Yes. We buy houses as-is, including ones with water damage. Share what you know about the damage and any insurance claims when you contact us.
